nameStory: Common whitlowgrass gets its peculiar name from an old folk belief that it could cure whitlows - painful infections around fingernails and toes. The 'grass' part is misleading since it's actually a member of the mustard family, not a true grass at all. This tiny plant was once considered so valuable for treating these finger ailments that people would seek it out specifically for medicinal purposes.
description: Common whitlowgrass is a tiny spring annual that you might easily overlook if you're not looking carefully. This diminutive plant grows only 1-4 inches tall and forms small rosettes of leaves at ground level. Despite its small size, it produces delicate white flowers that seem almost too big for such a little plant. It's one of our earliest spring bloomers, often appearing on bare patches of soil, sidewalk cracks, and stone walls when most other plants are still dormant.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers with four deeply notched petals that look almost heart-shaped or split in two, giving each flower an 8-petaled appearance. The flowers are only about 1/8 inch across but stand out brightly against the small green leaves.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small spoon-shaped leaves arranged in a flat rosette at ground level, each leaf about the size of your pinky fingernail. The leaves feel slightly fuzzy and have a few small teeth along the edges.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms tiny, low-growing rosettes that hug the ground, rarely taller than a few inches. Multiple small flower stems rise up from the center of each rosette, making the plant look like a miniature bouquet.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small oval seed pods (called silicles) that are flattened and about the size of a grain of rice. The pods split open when ripe to release tiny seeds.

habitat: Look for common whitlowgrass in disturbed, bare soil areas like sidewalk cracks, gravel paths, stone walls, and thin spots in lawns. It thrives in sunny locations with poor, sandy, or gravelly soil where larger plants can't compete. You'll often find it growing alongside other small weeds in parking lots, driveways, and along building foundations throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: This is when common whitlowgrass truly shines, blooming from March through May depending on your location. The tiny white flowers appear very early, sometimes even poking through late snow.
seasonality.summer: By early summer, the plants have usually completed their life cycle and disappeared entirely, leaving behind only scattered seeds in the soil for next year.
seasonality.fall: Nothing visible above ground - the plant exists only as seeds waiting in the soil for the next spring's growing season.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent above ground, but seeds lie dormant in cracks and crevices, ready to sprout when warm weather returns.

funFact: This tiny plant is actually a master of time travel - it can complete its entire life cycle from seed to flower to new seeds in just 4-6 weeks, making it one of the fastest-living flowering plants in New England and allowing it to 'time-share' habitats with larger plants that haven't even started growing yet.
confusionNotes: The deeply split white petals are your best clue to distinguish it from other tiny white spring flowers - most other small flowers have solid, unnotched petals. If the petals look heart-shaped or split down the middle, you've likely found common whitlowgrass.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name, this isn't a grass at all but belongs to the mustard family, the same group that includes broccoli, cabbage, and actual mustard plants. The 'grass' confusion probably arose because early botanists used 'grass' as a catch-all term for many small, inconspicuous plants.
compareHints: Common whitlowgrass differs from its relatives rock whitlow-mustard and wood whitlow-grass primarily by its habitat preferences and timing. While common whitlowgrass loves disturbed, bare ground and blooms very early, rock whitlow-mustard prefers actual rocky areas, and wood whitlow-grass grows in shadier forest settings. The deeply notched white petals are shared among all the whitlowgrasses, making habitat your best identification clue.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Rock whitlow-mustard differs from common whitlowgrass by its preference for rocky habitats (common whitlowgrass grows in disturbed soil and gardens) and its more robust, perennial-like appearance.
Wood Whitlow-grass differs from Common Whitlow-grass by having more stem leaves and preferring shaded forest habitats instead of sunny, disturbed ground.
